notes:
Method: built the CLI from source (go1.26.1) to /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-skill-do-work/213e30ac-5958-56c8-9fd2-faaaaf9c4ea6/scratchpad/audit596/dwcli and ran `DO_WORK_COMPATIBILITY_SHIM=1 dwcli --format text protected-inventory start|associate` against four throwaway repos in the same directory (repo = renames plus secret patterns, r2 = association conflicts, r3 = copy and ambiguity promotion, r4 = secret-derived deletion). Nothing in /home/user/skill-do-work was written.

Both known-false claims are confirmed: line 57 (`*credentials*` vs the code's singular `credential`) and line 72 ("An archived REQ outranks an in-flight one", where the active flag at inventory.go:281 is stored and never read). The same pass found six more, four of them in the two by-hand fallbacks a reader executes when the tool is gone: the associate half of line 47 (unowned candidates get no row at all), the raw-status-output claim at line 66 (the tool drops untracked hidden files under do-work/), the origin-classification instruction at line 66 (a non-secret rename origin never gets a row), the quarantine sentence at line 66 (start replaces the file and performs no overlay), the status filter at line 76 (working REQs are included whatever their status), and the globs at line 76 (they need globstar and still miss the 10 archived REQs sitting directly in do-work/archive/). Two defects of the REQ-555 shape appear here: line 59 says "Read each tag class this way, and no other way" and then covers four of the five tags in the legend directly above it, leaving X — including an ordinary file promoted by the ambiguity rule — with no rule; and line 55 defines XD as a deleted secret-shaped path when the code also tags a deleted secret-derived path XD, the case the X bullet one line up does name.

Out of section, same defect family, not fixed by this request: skills/do-work/actions/commit.md:85 and skills/do-work-toolbox/actions/inspect.md:117 both say associate "prints one `<owner>\\t<path>` row per candidate — a `REQ-NNN` id, or `-` for unassociated"; the wrapper prints no row for an unowned candidate, so commit.md's "Files that come back `-`" branch is unreachable. Separately, inspect.md:64 and :114 call `protected-inventory.sh start "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)" do-work-inspect-secret-quarantine`, and the launcher forwards positionals unchanged; the command accepts only --dry-run and --quarantine-name, so that call fails with "unknown option /path" and exit 2 (verified). That contradicts line 24's "most launchers translate a legacy positional call into the flags the subcommand requires", which belongs to the Shipped executable homes section, not mine.

claims.claim: "Publication here makes the [Verified exact publication](#verified-exact-publication) check, and so does the screenshot install that shares these mechanics: each verifies the path it actually wrote, removes only its own nested artifact, and exits nonzero with the occupying directory untouched."
claims.what_the_code_does: Three clauses generalized over two commands that behave differently. Clause 1, "verifies the path it actually wrote": TRUE of capture-screenshot only — it byte-compares source against its staged copy and then confirms the published name is the same inode it staged. FALSE of atomic-download — after os.Rename the only stat reads the size for the recorded change and its error is discarded; there is no byte or identity check, so the rename's exit status is exactly what it trusts, which is the thing the Verified exact publication section says is not proof. Clause 2, "removes only its own nested artifact": TRUE of NEITHER — neither command can nest anything. atomic-download refuses a directory target before it fetches, and its os.Rename would fail anyway; capture-screenshot refuses any existing destination before it stages, and its rooted link would fail anyway. I confirmed both syscalls empirically: rename onto a directory and linkat onto an existing name both return EEXIST and leave the directory with zero entries. What each actually removes on failure is its own adjacent staging file. Clause 3, "exits nonzero with the occupying directory untouched": TRUE of both, by different codes — atomic-download returns OutcomeFindings (exit 1), capture-screenshot returns OutcomeFailure (exit 2). Also "shares these mechanics" is wrong: the download is curl plus a clobbering rename, the screenshot is a verified private copy plus a no-clobber link. The final sentence of line 124 about the staged source is accurate and should survive.

Empirical syscall check (Go 1.25, scratchpad program): "os.Rename over dir: file exists / dir entries after rename: 0" and "Root.Link onto dir: linkat ... file exists / dir entries after link: 0".
claims.suggested_text: The two publications answer the [Verified exact publication](#verified-exact-publication) check differently, and only one of them verifies. The screenshot install byte-compares its private copy against the source, publishes it with a link that will not clobber, and then confirms the published name is the same file it staged; a destination that already exists, directory or not, is refused before anything is staged. That is what protects the staged source, since a staged capture is removed only after a publication that verifiably happened. The download inspects nothing afterwards: it refuses a target that is already a directory before it fetches, and then trusts the rename, which fails rather than descending into a directory the way `mv` would. claims.claim: A step calls `tools/do-work-cli.sh … record-timing-event` for a completed interval, or `tools/do-work-cli.sh … run-timed-command` for a command the suite launches and measures itself.
claims.what_the_code_does: Both subcommands are registered under exactly those names and behave as described: record-timing-event appends one already-completed interval, run-timed-command executes argv and measures both ends in-process.
claims.evidence: internal/lifecycletiming/timing_commands.go:16-18 defines CommandRecordTimingEvent = "record-timing-event" and CommandRunTimedCommand = "run-timed-command"; internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:144-148 RunTimedCommand "executes argv, measures it in-process".

claims.claim: "Both own the clock, so no caller derives a timestamp with `date` and no caller invents a second duration format."
claims.what_the_code_does: True of run-timed-command, which reads the clock at both ends itself. Not true of record-timing-event: it accepts `--started-at <RFC3339>` from the caller, and the shipped action that uses it passes one. actions/work.md Step 5 says to "take the current UTC instant (Timestamp rule) and hold it" and then record the interval with `--category builder-work --started-at <the instant you held>`; the Timestamp rule's option 2 is literally `date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ`. So a caller does derive a timestamp with `date` on the POSIX floor path. Only the duration format half is true of both.
claims.evidence: internal/lifecycletiming/timing_commands.go:171-176 parses `--started-at` as RFC3339 into options.startedAt/hasStartedAt; internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:278-281 uses that explicit start instead of chaining. Caller: skills/do-work/actions/work.md:284 passes `--started-at <the instant you held>`; skills/do-work/actions/work-reference.md:67-68 gives `do-work-cli.sh --format text now` first and `date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ` as the emergency floor.
claims.suggested_text: Both own the elapsed derivation and the one stream format, so no caller invents a second duration shape. `run-timed-command` owns the clock outright — it reads both ends itself. `record-timing-event` chains a boundary event to the previous event's end when no start is given, and takes an explicit `--started-at` only for a delegated interval whose start the caller already held, obtained through the Timestamp rule rather than a hand-rolled format.

claims.claim: "The wrapper attaches the child's own stdout and stderr to the console rather than a pipe".
claims.what_the_code_does: The wrapper sets both `command.Stdout` and `command.Stderr` to one writer, and main passes `os.Stderr` for it. The child's stdout is therefore merged onto the CLI's stderr, not left on stdout — deliberately, so stdout stays free for the rendered CommandResult. "Rather than a pipe" is correct; "stdout and stderr to the console" is true of stderr and only indirectly of stdout, and a caller who redirects the CLI's stdout captures the JSON result, never the wrapped gate's output.
claims.evidence: internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:167-168 `command.Stdout = childOutput` and `command.Stderr = childOutput`; internal/lifecycletiming/timing_commands.go:22-23 "childOutput receives a wrapped command's own stdout and stderr, which keeps stdout free for the rendered CommandResult; main passes os.Stderr"; cmd/do-work-cli/main.go:47 `lifecycletiming.Handlers(os.Stderr)`.
claims.suggested_text: The wrapper hands the child the CLI's own stderr handle for both its stdout and its stderr rather than a pipe — that keeps the CLI's stdout free for the rendered result — and exits with the child's status:

claims.claim: "exits with the child's status: the child's own code, 128 plus the signal number when a signal killed it, and 127 when the command never launched."
claims.what_the_code_does: childExitStatus returns the child's own exit code when it exited normally, and signalExitStatusBase (128) plus the signal number when Signaled(). A command that never launched returns timedCommandNotLaunchedStatus (127). Each of those becomes the process exit status through ExitCodeOverride, which the runtime honours for any value 1..255.
claims.evidence: internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:52-53 (127 and 128 constants), :213-226 childExitStatus, :178-180 the 127 launch path; internal/lifecycletiming/timing_commands.go:108/120/125 set ExitCodeOverride; internal/commandruntime/command_runtime.go:74-75 returns it verbatim.

claims.claim: "A command reaches the stream as its executable's base name plus an argv token count, never as arguments, so a token or a user-controlled path cannot land in durable evidence."
claims.what_the_code_does: The first half holds: redactCommandIdentity emits only `<base name> (N argv tokens)`, and record-timing-event's `--command` text is reduced the same way. The trailing conclusion does not generalize. `--operation`, `--agent` and `--revision` are free caller text that reaches the stream and the folded `## Timing` section as written; boundEvidenceText only strips control characters and `|`, collapses whitespace, and cuts at 120 runes — it does not redact tokens or paths. RenderTimingSection prints the operation into the request file, which is committed evidence.
claims.evidence: internal/lifecycletiming/lifecycle_timing.go:702-710 redactCommandIdentity; :716-731 boundEvidenceText (control-character strip plus a 120-rune bound, evidenceTextLimit at :104); :307 CommandIdentity is the only redacted field while Operation/Revision/ResponsibleAgent pass through; :498-505 RenderTimingSection writes SlowestStage.Operation and SlowestCommand.Operation into the `## Timing` section.
claims.suggested_text: Timing evidence is metadata only where the command itself is concerned. A command reaches the stream as its executable's base name plus an argv token count, never as arguments, so no argument value can land in durable evidence. The caller-written `--operation`, `--agent` and `--revision` labels are the exception and travel as written into both the stream and the folded `## Timing` section, stripped only of control characters and cut to 120 characters — so never put a token or a user-controlled path in one.

An absent stream is not an error and changes no bytes.

claims.claim: "the diff-tree form above is the suite default for path-only consumers."
claims.what_the_code_does: There are three path-only diff-tree consumers in the shipped Go and they use three different forms; none matches the form printed above. gateevidence adds `-z`. finalization drops `-m` entirely. gittransaction drops `-m` and adds `--root` and `-z`. Only one of the three carries the `-m` that the prescribed form makes central.
claims.evidence: internal/gateevidence/gate_evidence.go:377 `diff-tree --no-commit-id --name-only -r -m -z <commit>`; internal/finalization/finalization_apply.go:545 `diff-tree --no-commit-id --name-only -r <candidate>`; internal/gittransaction/git_transaction.go:1368 `diff-tree --root --no-commit-id --name-only -r -z <commitSHA>`.
claims.suggested_text: `-m` is what makes the form work on a merge, and `-z` is what makes it safe for a filename carrying a space, quote or newline. Shipped consumers add what their own input needs: `gateevidence` reads arbitrary commits after a green gate and carries both flags, while `gittransaction` reads a commit it just created and carries `--root -z` without `-m`. Take the flags from the input, not from a single house form.

The probe really is cwd-relative in practice, because the handler runs `git -C <RepositoryRoot> check-ignore` and RepositoryRoot defaults to the process working directory when `--repo-root` is not passed — which the retained launcher never passes.

claims.claim: "Whenever a publication's destination could already be occupied, the publishing step verifies the path it actually wrote; the rename's or link's exit status is not that proof" — extended at line 108 to "every publication described below".

The two that skip verification are safe for a different reason — Go's syscalls refuse an occupied destination — but they do exactly what this sentence says is not proof.
claims.evidence: Verifies: internal/corehelpers/publication.go:176-181 (`parentRoot.Link`, then Stat both names and `os.SameFile`). Does not verify: internal/corehelpers/commands.go:888-892 (`os.Rename` then `info, _ := os.Stat(targetPath)` for the size only); internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:184-204 (`parent.Rename` / `parent.Link`, `keep = true`, return).
claims.suggested_text: Whenever a publication's destination could already be occupied, the publishing step must be able to name what it actually wrote. `capture-screenshot` proves it outright, re-stating the destination against its own stage with `os.SameFile` after the link. `atomic-download` and `publish-portfolio-summary` take the proof from the syscall instead, which refuses an occupied destination rather than writing under it. Both answer the same check; shell written by hand has neither and must verify the path itself.

claims.claim: "`ln` and `mv` treat a directory standing in the destination's place as a container rather than a collision, so the payload lands inside it under the private staging name, the command exits zero, and the destination is still the directory it was."
claims.what_the_code_does: This describes shell that no longer runs in any publication path. Every shipped publication publishes through Go — os.Rename, os.Link, or os.Root.Link — and all three refuse an occupied destination instead of nesting under it. I confirmed this on the same filesystem: os.Rename, os.Link and Root.Link each returned "file exists" against a directory destination and wrote nothing, while shell `mv` and `ln` both exited 0 and deposited the staging file inside the directory. The one remaining shell `mv` in the suite is in the installer's bootstrap heredoc, into a fresh mktemp directory, not a publication.
claims.evidence: internal/corehelpers/publication.go:176 `parentRoot.Link(...)`; internal/corehelpers/commands.go:889 `os.Rename(temporaryPath, targetPath)`; internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:190/196 `parent.Rename` / `parent.Link`; internal/atomicfile/atomic_replace_unix.go:8 `os.Rename`. Measured: Go -> "rename ...: file exists", "link ...: file exists", "linkat ...: file exists"; shell -> `mv` exit 0 and `ln` exit 0, both leaving `.dest.publishing.*` inside `dest/`. Only shell mv left: skills/do-work/tools/install-do-work-suite.sh:25, inside the bootstrap heredoc.
claims.suggested_text: Go's `os.Rename` and `os.Link` refuse a destination that already exists, so no shipped publication can nest its payload inside an occupying directory or exit zero over one. Shell does the opposite — `mv` and `ln` treat that directory as a container, land the payload inside it under the private staging name, and exit zero with the destination still the directory it was — so hand-written shell has to make the check that the syscall makes for the helpers.

claims.claim: "The shipped helper downloads to a private adjacent temporary file, publishes by rename only after curl succeeds, and preserves failures".
claims.what_the_code_does: handleAtomicDownload creates a temp file with os.CreateTemp in the target's own directory (mode 0600), runs curl into it, and only on curl exit zero renames it onto the target. Every failure path returns without publishing and the deferred Remove discards the stage. It also refuses up front when the target is an existing directory. Note: this is the corehelpers curl route, not archivefetch.DownloadAtomic, which is the installer's separate net/http path.
claims.evidence: internal/corehelpers/commands.go:869-892; the directory pre-check at :868.

claims.claim: The helper retries with `--retry 3 --retry-delay 2 --retry-max-time 60`.
claims.what_the_code_does: Those four flags are passed verbatim to curl, alongside `-fsSL`.
claims.evidence: internal/corehelpers/commands.go:879 `curlArguments := []string{"-fsSL", "--retry", "3", "--retry-delay", "2", "--retry-max-time", "60"}`.

claims.claim: "When `GH_TOKEN` or `GITHUB_TOKEN` is non-empty the helper sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; absent or empty, the request goes out exactly as it would without them."
claims.what_the_code_does: The helper takes the first non-empty of GH_TOKEN then GITHUB_TOKEN and appends `-H "Authorization: Bearer <token>"` only in that case; with neither set the curl argv is unchanged.
claims.evidence: internal/corehelpers/commands.go:880-882 with firstNonempty at :895-902.

claims.claim: "The canonical command copies and verifies that source into a private file adjacent to the canonical target, once per output."
claims.what_the_code_does: Two things are off. The source is read once into memory, not copied once per output, and each output is written from that one buffer. And the private staging file sits adjacent to the output being published, not adjacent to the canonical target — for `--with-snapshot` the snapshot's stage is created in the snapshot directory, which is a different directory from the canonical file's. There is also no read-back verification of the staged bytes; the only verification before a replace is that the existing canonical target is unchanged.
claims.evidence: internal/toolboxcommands/portfolio.go:31 `data, readErr := os.ReadFile(source)` — the single read; :120 and :143 both call rootedPublishFile with that same `data`. internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:140-141 the stage's parent is `filepath.Dir(relative)` of the output being published; :162 `temporary := "." + leaf + ".publishing-" + hex...`; :184-189 the pre-replace check compares the target against itself, not the stage against the source. Caller directories differ: skills/do-work-toolbox/actions/present-work.md:133-134 (canonical `do-work/deliverables/portfolio-summary.md`, snapshot under `do-work/deliverables/portfolio-snapshots/`).
claims.suggested_text: The canonical command reads that source once and publishes every output from those same bytes, staging each one in a private file adjacent to its own target — the snapshot beside the snapshot, the canonical beside the canonical.

claims.claim: "`--canonical-only` atomically replaces only the canonical file. `--with-snapshot` first publishes an exclusive snapshot from its own verified copy, advances occupied candidates with numeric suffixes, and only then atomically replaces the canonical file from the same bytes."
claims.what_the_code_does: Modes and ordering match. --canonical-only touches one path. --with-snapshot loops for the first free candidate (`-2`, `-3`, … before the extension), publishes it exclusively via a no-clobber link, and only then publishes the canonical from the same in-memory bytes.
claims.evidence: internal/toolboxcommands/portfolio.go:22-27 mode parsing and arity; :110-133 the snapshot loop, breaking only after a successful exclusive publish; :134-149 the canonical publish afterwards; firstFreePortfolioPath at :198-215 for the numeric suffixes; internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:196 `parent.Link` for the exclusive create.

claims.claim: "Missing, failed, or malformed canonical tooling stops the caller; the retained toolbox script is not a fallback."
claims.what_the_code_does: There is no retained toolbox script — for portfolio publication or anything else. skills/do-work-toolbox contains only SKILL.md, actions/, crew-members/ and docs/; it ships no scripts/ or tools/ directory at all, and no file named for portfolio publication exists anywhere in the suite outside the Go package. The sentence names an artifact that does not exist. The instruction it carries (do not fall back) is still right, so only the naming needs to go.
claims.evidence: `ls -R skills/do-work-toolbox` -> SKILL.md, actions, crew-members, docs only. `find skills -iname "*portfolio*"` -> internal/toolboxcommands/portfolio.go and portfolio_test.go only. skills/do-work/scripts/ contains no publish-portfolio-summary launcher (11 scripts, none for portfolio).
claims.suggested_text: Missing, failed, or malformed canonical tooling stops the caller; there is no script fallback for this publication in either skill.

claims.claim: "The two outputs carry identical bytes but never share storage: a snapshot linked to the canonical file would follow every later in-place edit of it."
claims.what_the_code_does: Each output is written independently from the same in-memory buffer into its own private stage, then published. The hard link that rootedPublishFile uses only ever links a stage to its own leaf, never one output to another, so the two published files are separate inodes.
claims.evidence: internal/toolboxcommands/portfolio.go:120 and :143 — two separate rootedPublishFile calls with the same `data`; internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:163-196 — each call opens its own O_EXCL stage and links that stage to its own leaf.

claims.claim: "a snapshot candidate occupied by a directory advances to the next suffix, a canonical path occupied by a directory fails closed, and neither leaves a private file nested inside it."
claims.what_the_code_does: All three hold. firstFreePortfolioPath Lstats each candidate and skips anything that exists, directory included; if a publish still races, the loop re-checks and continues to the next suffix. An occupied canonical path is Lstat'd and rejected as unsafe when it is not a regular file, which exits 1. And no private file can nest, because the stage is created in the output's parent directory and the link/rename onto an occupied name fails rather than writing under it.
claims.evidence: internal/toolboxcommands/portfolio.go:207-214 (Lstat-and-advance), :121-126 (retry on a still-occupied candidate), :137-144 (`!info.Mode().IsRegular()` -> PORTFOLIO-CANONICAL-UNSAFE) and :84-86 in the transaction path; internal/resultmodel/result_model.go:652-653 maps OutcomeFindings to exit 1; internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:140-141 and :167-172 (stage in the output's parent, removed unless kept).

claims.claim: "An exclusive snapshot failure leaves the prior canonical unchanged. A later canonical replacement failure leaves the new snapshot published and reports that partial outcome. Existing snapshots are never truncated, replaced, or automatically removed."
claims.what_the_code_does: The snapshot is published before the canonical is touched, so a snapshot failure returns with the canonical untouched. A canonical failure after a published snapshot adds a second finding naming the retained snapshot. Snapshots are created with a no-clobber link onto a path that was Lstat-verified free, and nothing in the command removes an existing one.
claims.evidence: internal/toolboxcommands/portfolio.go:117-126 (snapshot failures return with "canonical was not changed"); :146-148 (canonical failure carries "snapshot retained when present"); :171-176 portfolioDirectFailure appends PORTFOLIO-SNAPSHOT-RETAINED "intentionally retained"; internal/toolboxcommands/mutation.go:196 uses Link (no overwrite) for the create path.

claims.claim: "An apostrophe is enough to break naïve single-quote interpolation; command syntax inside the text can then execute rather than remain data."
claims.what_the_code_does: This section prescribes a rule for action authors and names no shipped helper, so there is no Go implementation to compare it against. The shell claim itself is correct: an apostrophe inside a single-quoted string terminates the quote, leaving the rest of the text in command position.
claims.evidence: No shipped Go or shell command implements or contradicts this section — it is a rule for action prose, unlike every other section in this guide, which names a route or a command.

claims.claim: "`-x` matches file and directory basenames, so a same-named source directory disappears too."
claims.what_the_code_does: Verified against diff: with both a `generated/` directory and a `generated.png` file present in each tree, `diff -r -x generated` suppressed the directory's contents entirely while still reporting `generated.png` and `other.txt`. The exclusion is matched on basenames of both kinds.
claims.evidence: Scratch trees: `diff -r a b` reported generated/f.txt, generated.png and other.txt; `diff -r -x generated a b` reported only generated.png and other.txt.

claims.claim: "Prescribed command blocks are independent invocations. Shell variables, traps, and random `mktemp` paths from an earlier block are unavailable later … the action carries the literal in its durable/context record and re-types it."
claims.what_the_code_does: Nothing in the suite persists shell state between blocks — every mechanic that must survive is either re-derived deterministically from git or carried as a re-typed literal. The worktree dispatch sequence follows exactly that: both merge endpoints are held as literals and re-typed into each later command, and the reference gives the concrete failure of doing otherwise.
claims.evidence: skills/do-work/actions/work-reference.md:439 "a `\"$pre..$merge_hash\"` composed in a fresh shell expands to `\"..\"`, which git rejects"; skills/do-work/actions/work.md:310 "Hold both hashes … as literals you re-type into each later command (shell variables do not survive between command blocks)"; skills/do-work/actions/work-reference.md:420 applies the same holding rule to `<operative_name>`.

notes:
Scope note: the prompt's exclusion list removes the section containing line 124 (that is "## Atomic download publication", lines 110-124) but the pay-attention list names atomic download publication. I audited it anyway and report three claims from it (lines 112, 118, 120), all accurate — the guide's curl description is correct because `atomic-download` really does shell out to curl (internal/corehelpers/commands.go:879-887). Worth flagging for whoever merges the batch: there are TWO download implementations, and only one matches the guide. `archivefetch.DownloadAtomic` (internal/archivefetch/archive_fetch.go:153-180) is a net/http reimplementation with a hand-rolled 4-attempt loop, a 2s delay and a 60s budget, publishing by rooted hard link rather than rename; it serves the suite installer. If anyone ever re-points `atomic-download` at that package, every curl sentence in that section goes stale at once.

Highest-value findings, in order: (F1) line 106's `ln`/`mv` sentence is stale shell — every shipped publication uses Go's os.Rename/os.Link/Root.Link, which I measured returning "file exists" against a directory destination while shell mv and ln both exit 0 and nest the payload. (F2) line 92's "suite default" claim — three shipped diff-tree consumers, three different flag sets, none matching the printed form. (F3) line 128's "retained toolbox script" names a file that does not exist; do-work-toolbox ships no scripts/ or tools/ directory at all.

Three findings are the generalize-over-N defect class the batch targets: line 30 "Both own the clock, so no caller derives a timestamp with `date`" (true of run-timed-command, false of record-timing-event, whose shipped caller at actions/work.md:284 passes `--started-at` from the Timestamp rule whose floor is `date -u`); line 32 "a token or a user-controlled path cannot land in durable evidence" (true of the command argv, false of `--operation`/`--agent`/`--revision`, which reach the committed `## Timing` section as written); line 106/108 "the publishing step verifies the path it actually wrote … for every publication described below" (true of capture-screenshot only; atomic-download and publish-portfolio-summary rely on the syscall's own refusal, which is exactly the "exit status is not that proof" the sentence rules out).

Empirical checks I ran rather than reasoned about: git status collapsing an untracked directory, diff-tree/-m and `git show --name-only --format=` on a real merge, the `**/` prefix against a subdirectory probe, `git check-ignore --no-index` on a tracked path, `diff -x` on a same-named directory, and Go vs shell rename/link into an occupied directory. Scratch files are under the session scratchpad and touch nothing in the repository; I made no edits, stages, or commits.
